newsitem.title: USA: Glenn calls for Space Day in May.
newsitem.headline: Glenn calls for Space Day in May.

text.p: Former astronaut John Glenn marked the 35th anniversary of his flight around the Earth on Thursday by announcing plans for a national Space Day on May 22 to promote space exploration.
Glenn, now a Democratic senator from Ohio, became the first American to orbit Earth on Feb. 20, 1962.
He made three orbits in five hours before his Mercury spacecraft landed in the Atlantic Ocean near the Bahamas.

"The promise of space in exploration, discovery and the application of new technology is yet to be fulfilled and we must press on," Glenn said in a statement. "Space Day will give us a moment to celebrate and reflect together on the great achievements and future opportunities in space."

He and other organisers of Space Day hope it will be marked by programmes in schools and communities across the country. They have established an internet site with news about space at www.spaceday.com.

Events planned in Washington include dedication of a statue of an astronaut and special exhibits at the National Air and Space Museum. Space Day marks the anniversary of President John Kennedy's 1961 speech to Congress setting the goal of landing Americans on the Moon by the end of that decade. The first Moon landing took place on July 20, 1969.

Glenn, 75, was one of the first seven astronauts chosen in 1959. After leaving the space programme he was elected to the Senate in 1974 and has been re-elected three times. He was expected to announce in his home town of New Concord, Ohio, on Thursday whether he will seek a fifth term next year.
